concepts.label: Parametric memory
concepts.blurb: Knowledge a language model holds in its weights, which cannot be inspected or changed without retraining.

concepts.label: Non-parametric memory
concepts.blurb: Knowledge held outside the weights in a searchable index, which can be swapped or updated without touching the model.

concepts.label: The retriever and generator split
concepts.blurb: The two halves of a retrieval-augmented system, and what it means to train them together with no supervision on which document is right.

concepts.label: RAG-Sequence
concepts.blurb: The formulation that conditions a whole generated sequence on one retrieved document.

concepts.label: RAG-Token
concepts.blurb: The formulation that draws a different retrieved document for each generated token and marginalises over them.

concepts.label: Provenance and updating
concepts.blurb: The two problems that motivate retrieval: saying where an answer came from, and changing what a system knows.

concepts.label: Sparse retrieval
concepts.blurb: Ranking by weighted token overlap between query and document, which is what BM25 computes over high-dimensional sparse vectors.

concepts.label: Dense retrieval
concepts.blurb: Ranking by similarity between query and document embeddings produced by encoders trained for the task.

concepts.label: In-batch negatives
concepts.blurb: The training arrangement that treats every other passage in a batch as a negative example for the current query.

concepts.label: In-domain versus zero-shot
concepts.blurb: The distinction that decides whether a dense retriever beats a lexical baseline, and the reason benchmark rankings reverse.

concepts.label: Hybrid retrieval
concepts.blurb: Combining a lexical and a dense ranker, which the primary sources report improves on either alone in some settings.

concepts.label: Annotation artefact
concepts.blurb: A property of how a dataset was built, rather than of the task, that changes which retrieval method wins on it.

concepts.label: Precision and recall
concepts.blurb: The two base measures of retrieval effectiveness over an unranked result set, and what each fraction counts.

concepts.label: Recall at k
concepts.blurb: The fraction of relevant documents retrieved within a cutoff, and why the cutoff has to be stated with the number.

concepts.label: nDCG
concepts.blurb: Discounted cumulative gain normalised against the ideal ranking, which is the measure graded relevance judgements make possible.

concepts.label: Reciprocal rank
concepts.blurb: One divided by the position of the first relevant result, which suits tasks with a single right answer.

concepts.label: Graded versus binary relevance
concepts.blurb: Whether a judgement records relevant or not, or records how relevant, and which measures each one supports.

concepts.label: The evaluation cutoff
concepts.blurb: The k in a measure, which is a decision about the application rather than a property of the ranker.

concepts.label: Choosing a headline measure
concepts.blurb: Why a benchmark picks one number to rank systems by, and what that choice leaves out.

concepts.label: Fixed-size chunking
concepts.blurb: Splitting a document sequentially into chunks of a set length, which is the baseline every other strategy gets measured against.

concepts.label: Semantic chunking
concepts.blurb: Splitting on detected topic boundaries rather than on length, and what measuring it against the baseline actually showed.

concepts.label: Chunk overlap
concepts.blurb: Repeating text across chunk boundaries, and the trade-off between continuity and redundancy that repeating it creates.

concepts.label: Token-level evaluation
concepts.blurb: Scoring a chunking strategy by which tokens it retrieves rather than which chunks, so strategies with different chunk sizes stay comparable.

concepts.label: Measured versus advocated
concepts.blurb: The difference between a number somebody ran an experiment to get and a number somebody recommended, and how to tell them apart in a source.

concepts.label: A published default
concepts.blurb: A number a tool or a tutorial ships as its starting value, which carries no evidence with it unless the source supplies some.

concepts.label: Internal inconsistency in a source
concepts.blurb: One document recommending two different values for the same parameter, which is itself a signal about how the recommendation was reached.

concepts.label: Corpus dependence
concepts.blurb: The reason chunking advice cannot be stated as fact: the right value depends on the documents, and the sources say so themselves.

concepts.label: The position effect
concepts.blurb: Accuracy on a retrieval-augmented task depending on where in the input the relevant passage sits.

concepts.label: U-shaped attention bias
concepts.blurb: The measured tendency for tokens at the start and the end of an input to draw more attention regardless of their relevance.

concepts.label: The multi-document QA probe
concepts.blurb: The experimental design that isolates position: hold the documents fixed and move the one that contains the answer.

concepts.label: The key-value retrieval probe
concepts.blurb: A synthetic task with no semantic content, used to separate a retrieval failure from a comprehension failure.

concepts.label: Query-aware contextualisation
concepts.blurb: The intervention Lost in the Middle tested against the position effect, which nearly fixed one task and barely moved the other.

concepts.label: An architectural account
concepts.blurb: Explaining a behavioural effect from the model's structure rather than from its training data.

concepts.label: Reader saturation
concepts.blurb: Reader accuracy flattening while retriever recall is still climbing, which is what caps the useful number of passages.

concepts.label: Choosing k
concepts.blurb: How many passages to put in the context, treated as a measured trade-off rather than as a default.

concepts.label: The cost of a distractor
concepts.blurb: What adding an irrelevant passage does to accuracy, which is not nothing.

concepts.label: Degradation with input length
concepts.blurb: Reasoning accuracy falling as the input grows even with position held constant, which is a separate effect from position.

concepts.label: Contested evidence
concepts.blurb: What to do when primary sources disagree: state the disagreement, name the conditions each measured under, and cite both.

concepts.label: Reranking
concepts.blurb: Reordering retrieved passages before they reach the model, which is the practical consequence of the position effect.

concepts.label: Reflection tokens
concepts.blurb: Special vocabulary a model emits to say whether to retrieve and how good the result was, trained as ordinary next-token prediction.

concepts.label: Adaptive retrieval
concepts.blurb: Deciding at each step whether to retrieve at all, instead of retrieving a fixed number of passages every time.

concepts.label: The retrieval threshold
concepts.blurb: Turning a predicted token into a decision by comparing its probability against a bar somebody sets.

concepts.label: Interleaving reasoning and action
concepts.blurb: Alternating thoughts that change nothing outside the model with actions that do, so each one informs the other.

concepts.label: The agentic loop
concepts.blurb: A system that chooses its own retrieval queries as part of reasoning, rather than running a fixed pipeline.

concepts.label: The ablation baseline
concepts.blurb: Comparing against the same method with one half removed, which is what makes a claim about the combination mean anything.

concepts.label: Document conversion
concepts.blurb: Turning a page-oriented format back into structured machine-readable content, and why the format makes that hard.

concepts.label: Document layout analysis
concepts.blurb: Deciding which regions of a page are which kind of element, and how those regions group into reading units.

concepts.label: The layout label set
concepts.blurb: The classes a layout dataset commits to, and how that choice decides what a model trained on it can learn.

concepts.label: Layout domain shift
concepts.blurb: A layout model trained on uniformly typeset documents failing on documents that are not, and why the training corpus caused it.

concepts.label: Reading order
concepts.blurb: The sequence a page's content should be read in, which the file format does not record.

concepts.label: Pipeline composition
concepts.blurb: A working conversion system built as an assembly of specialised models rather than as one end-to-end model.

concepts.label: Inter-annotator agreement
concepts.blurb: How far two people labelling the same data agree, measured with the same metric the model is scored with.

concepts.label: The human ceiling
concepts.blurb: The score that agreement between annotators sets, which is the target a model is actually chasing rather than a perfect score.

concepts.label: Redundant annotation
concepts.blurb: Labelling the same items more than once on purpose, which is the only way an agreement number can be computed at all.

concepts.label: Ground-truth ambiguity
concepts.blurb: Cases with more than one defensible correct answer, which put a hard limit on any evaluation that admits only one.

concepts.label: The annotation guideline
concepts.blurb: The written rules that turn a labelling task into a repeatable one, and what consistency looks like without them.

concepts.label: Annotator qualification
concepts.blurb: Screening and training labellers before their work counts, and the attrition that screening produces.

concepts.label: Annotation independence
concepts.blurb: Keeping labellers from seeing each other's work, without which an agreement number measures conformity instead.

concepts.label: OCR with a vision language model
concepts.blurb: Reading a page with a model that takes the image and produces text, rather than with a character-recognition pipeline.

concepts.label: Document anchoring
concepts.blurb: Feeding a model the element coordinates the file already records alongside the page image, so it is not working from pixels alone.

concepts.label: Linearisation
concepts.blurb: Flattening a two-dimensional page into a single sequence of text in a defensible order.

concepts.label: Unit tests as a reward
concepts.blurb: Scoring an output by how many checkable assertions it satisfies, which works where no single correct output exists.

concepts.label: Synthetic training documents
concepts.blurb: Generating pages whose ground truth is known because the generator wrote it.

concepts.label: Cost per page
concepts.blurb: The number that decides whether a conversion pipeline can run over a corpus, and why quoting it means naming a version.

concepts.label: Inherited failure modes
concepts.blurb: A distilled model's residual errors tracing back to the model that produced its training data.

concepts.label: Test collection
concepts.blurb: The documents, the information needs, and the relevance judgements that together make a retrieval score reproducible.

concepts.label: Marginal relevance
concepts.blurb: A document scored for what it adds to the set already chosen, rather than for its similarity to the query alone.

concepts.label: Diversity against relevance
concepts.blurb: The choice between filling a result set with the closest matches and covering more of what the query could have meant.

concepts.label: The diversity parameter
concepts.blurb: The single number that places a diversity-aware ranker between pure relevance and pure novelty, and what each endpoint produces.

concepts.label: Ranking score against answer score
concepts.blurb: Measuring the ranking is not measuring what the model wrote from it, and a gain in one need not be a gain in the other.

concepts.label: Best-of-sweep reporting
concepts.blurb: Reporting a method at the best point of a parameter sweep, and what that hides about how it behaves everywhere else.

concepts.label: Shared dataset dependence
concepts.blurb: Two studies that reuse one benchmark and one setup are one result reported twice, not two confirmations.

concepts.label: Evidence gap
concepts.blurb: A question the literature has not answered, named as an absence rather than filled with a plausible number.

concepts.label: Single-time retrieval
concepts.blurb: Retrieving once from the user's input and generating the whole answer from what came back, and the questions that defeats.

concepts.label: Fixed-schedule interleaving
concepts.blurb: Retrieving again on a schedule the system sets, every so many tokens or every reasoning step, regardless of what the model needs.

concepts.label: Model-decided interleaving
concepts.blurb: Letting the generator choose when to stop and fetch, from its own confidence or its own emitted question.

concepts.label: Query complexity routing
concepts.blurb: Choosing the retrieval strategy before generation starts, from a prediction about how hard the question is.

concepts.label: Just-in-time context
concepts.blurb: Holding identifiers rather than content and loading the content at the moment it is needed.

concepts.label: Interleaving overhead
concepts.blurb: What repeated retrieval costs in activations, latency and recomputation, and why the sources state it rather than measure it.

concepts.label: Baseline mismatch
concepts.blurb: Two results are not comparable when each was measured against a different baseline, however alike their headline numbers look.

concepts.label: Graph state
concepts.blurb: A single shared object every node reads from and writes to, whose schema is the graph's parameter.

concepts.label: State reducer
concepts.blurb: The two-argument function that decides how an update to one state key combines with what is already there.

concepts.label: Nodes and edges
concepts.blurb: The split between the functions that do work and the wiring that decides which one runs next.

concepts.label: Conditional edge
concepts.blurb: Routing chosen at run time by a function of the state, which is how a loop and a branch are expressed in a graph.

concepts.label: Builder against compiled graph
concepts.blurb: The object you assemble is not the object you run, and what compiling is for.

concepts.label: Version-pinned documentation
concepts.blurb: Citing a moving document by the version and the date it was read, because it will say something else later.

concepts.label: Checkpoint
concepts.blurb: A snapshot of the whole graph state at one point in a run, written where the runtime says a step boundary is.

concepts.label: Thread identity
concepts.blurb: The key that decides which accumulated state a run joins, and what reusing or not reusing it buys.

concepts.label: Super-step
concepts.blurb: The unit of execution a checkpoint is written after, which is what makes persistence granularity a decision rather than an accident.

concepts.label: Replay and resume
concepts.blurb: Restarting from a saved checkpoint, and knowing exactly which work is skipped and which runs again.

concepts.label: Node idempotency
concepts.blurb: Writing node logic that can run twice without corrupting anything, because persistence makes re-execution ordinary.

concepts.label: Interrupt and resume
concepts.blurb: Pausing a run from inside a node, surfacing a value to the caller, and continuing from a value the caller supplies.

concepts.label: Durability mode
concepts.blurb: When state is actually written, and the trade between losing work and paying for the write.

concepts.label: LLM as judge
concepts.blurb: Using a language model to score another model's output, and how agreement with human judgement is defined before it is measured.

concepts.label: Judge bias
concepts.blurb: The measured failure modes of a model judge: order, length, self-preference, and questions it cannot grade.

concepts.label: Judge validation
concepts.blurb: Checking a judge against task-specific human labels before trusting it, and how far a validated judge transfers.

concepts.label: Reference-free evaluation
concepts.blurb: Scoring a retrieval-augmented answer without a gold answer, by decomposing it and checking each part against the retrieved context.

concepts.label: Offline replay
concepts.blurb: Measuring a system by running a fixed question set against a fixed corpus, and what that design can and cannot establish.

concepts.label: Live traffic measurement
concepts.blurb: Measuring a deployed system from what real users do, and why the two modes answer different questions.

concepts.label: A/B test
concepts.blurb: Splitting live traffic between one change and the current system, and the traffic it needs before it says anything.

concepts.label: Paired comparison
concepts.blurb: Showing one user both variants at once and reading the preference off their actions, which needs far less traffic than splitting them.

concepts.label: Ground truth as a proxy
concepts.blurb: Every evaluation scores against a stand-in somebody chose, and an unexamined stand-in quietly decides what counts as a failure.
